ocar.opportunity: Psychiatry and systems neuroscience need a shared language for brain wiring: a complete map of neural elements and their links, at a chosen scale, that can be compared across people and clinical states.
ocar.challenge: Neural elements may be neurons or areas, and links may be synapses or inter-areal pathways, so the same word 'connectome' covers very different maps. How structural topology relates to dynamics, development, and disease is still being organized rather than settled.
ocar.action: O. Sporns contributes a chapter in the New Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry (2020) surveying origins and definitions of the connectome, structural versus functional connectivity, human network topology, dynamics, and individual differences in development and clinical populations.
ocar.resolution: The chapter frames connectome maps as complete, systematic accounts of anatomical or physiological relationships at a given scale, and uses that frame to review topology, how connectivity shapes activity, and clinical/developmental themes. It is an overview, not a new reconstruction.
ocar.future_work: The abstract points to ongoing work on individual differences, development, and clinical populations rather than stating a specific experimental next step.

summaries.beginner: A connectome is a complete map of how brain parts are wired together, whether those parts are single cells or whole regions. This textbook chapter explains where the idea came from, what human brain networks look like, and how wiring relates to activity, development, and psychiatric illness.
summaries.intermediate: In the New Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry (2020), O. Sporns reviews the origins and definitions of the connectome and its application to structural and functional connectivity. The chapter surveys major findings on human connectome topology, how connectivity structure shapes dynamic brain activity, and themes in individual differences, development, and clinical populations.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. This is a textbook overview, not an original experiment. The abstract does not enumerate which topology findings, datasets, or clinical results are covered, and no sample sizes or network metrics are given.

plain_language_summary: A connectome is a complete map of how brain parts are wired together, whether those parts are single cells or whole regions. This textbook chapter explains where the idea came from, what human brain networks look like, and how wiring relates to activity, development, and psychiatric illness.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain synaptic maps, first completed for C. elegans, are becoming available for larval and adult Drosophila and could organize decades of fly circuit work into a single wiring framework.
ocar.challenge: In a whole brain it is hard to isolate what distinct circuits contribute, because even early sensory layers are synaptically interconnected and higher regions are densely linked by long-range projections and multisensory convergence. Communication beyond direct synapses also remains to be understood.
ocar.action: K. Vogt writes in Journal of Neurogenetics (2020) about forthcoming Janelia larval and adult Drosophila whole-brain connectomes, the C. elegans 302-neuron precedent, and how fly genetics and behavior can turn those maps into a functional connectome.
ocar.resolution: The piece argues that complete wiring shows sensory processing is not confined to separate channels, that higher brain regions are densely interconnected, and that Drosophila can still pursue whole-brain function by combining connectomics with genetic tools and behavioral paradigms.
ocar.future_work: The abstract flags neuronal communication beyond direct synaptic modulation, and using the forthcoming whole-brain maps together with genetics and behavior, as the work still needed.

summaries.beginner: After the tiny worm C. elegans, researchers are finishing full wiring maps of fruit-fly brains. This essay argues those maps will matter most when combined with fly genetics and behavior, because even early sensory circuits talk to one another rather than running in isolated lanes.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Neurogenetics (2020), K. Vogt discusses upcoming larval and adult Drosophila whole-brain connectomes from Janelia Research Campus, following the C. elegans reconstruction of a 302-neuron nervous system. The essay argues that earliest sensory layers are strongly synaptically interconnected, that long-range projections densely link higher regions and multisensory convergence centers, and that non-synaptic communication still needs study—all tractable in Drosophila with genetic tools and behavioral paradigms.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. This is a perspective, not a completed reconstruction; Janelia whole-brain maps are described as forthcoming. No synapse counts, circuit diagrams, or new experimental results appear in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: After the tiny worm C. elegans, researchers are finishing full wiring maps of fruit-fly brains. This essay argues those maps will matter most when combined with fly genetics and behavior, because even early sensory circuits talk to one another rather than running in isolated lanes.

ocar.opportunity: Connectome databases are often built by collating tract-tracing papers. If experts extract connections reliably, those matrices can support network analysis of neuronal dynamics and brain function.
ocar.challenge: Tract-tracing descriptions are often not clear-cut and interregional documentation is not standardized, so different experts may interpret the same paper differently. Large extraction variability could misconstruct adjacency matrices and fault graph analyses. No prior study had quantified that variability.
ocar.action: Schmitt, Eipert, Schwanke, Lessmann, Meinhardt, Beier, and colleagues report in Briefings in Bioinformatics (2019) an inter-rater study: three blinded experts extract hypothalamic connections from 16 tract-tracing publications, with a workflow to detect variability across processing steps.
ocar.resolution: Variability among the three experts was found. The authors analyze observation scores, matrix visualizations of discrepant connections, and weight variations in adjacency matrices, and release data and software via NeuroVIISAS.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents the workflow as a way to detect connectivity variability in connectome metastudies; applying it beyond this 16-paper hypothalamic sample is the implied next use.

summaries.beginner: Brain-wiring databases are often built by people reading old tracing papers and typing connections into a table. This study asks whether different experts read the same papers the same way, using hypothalamic connections as a test case.
summaries.intermediate: In Briefings in Bioinformatics (2019), Schmitt, Eipert, Schwanke, Lessmann, Meinhardt, Beier, Kadir, Karnitzki, Sellner, Klünker, Ruß, and Jenssen compare three blinded experts extracting connections from 16 tract-tracing papers on hypothalamic subregions. They propose a workflow to detect variability at processing steps and analyze observation scores, discrepant-connection matrices, and adjacency-matrix weight variation. Data and software are pointed to NeuroVIISAS.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Variability is reported as present among three raters, but the abstract does not give agreement statistics, percentages, or which connections disagreed. Results are limited to a 16-paper hypothalamic example.

plain_language_summary: Brain-wiring databases are often built by people reading old tracing papers and typing connections into a table. This study asks whether different experts read the same papers the same way, using hypothalamic connections as a test case.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomes of the brain are common, but few exist for the human spinal cord. A draft connectivity map could serve as a template for specialized behavioral calibrations and as the basis for an initial computational model, including studies of stimulation for pain relief.
ocar.challenge: Human data on cell types, connectivity, and connection strength are incomplete, so other species must be substituted. Neuron counts must be estimated from cadaveric measurements, histology, and cytoarchitecture rather than counted in a living cord.
ocar.action: Arle, Iftimia, Shils, Mei, and Carlson report in Neural Computation (2019) a literature-derived draft human spinal cord connectome and neural-circuitry simulations covering all ten Rexed laminae across 31 segments, applied to spinal cord stimulation for analgesia.
ocar.resolution: The model includes intralaminar, interlaminar, and intersegmental connections plus ascending and descending brain links, with estimated neuron counts by cell type in every lamina of all 31 segments. The authors note highly interconnected recurrent networks and present the model as a starting point for biomedical hypotheses.
ocar.future_work: Each application needs additional calibrations to constrain output to verifiable predictions. The authors state that future work will include simulating additional segments and expanding the research uses of the model.

summaries.beginner: Most wiring maps are of the brain, not the spinal cord. This team builds a first-pass computer model of human spinal circuits from published anatomy and uses it to study electrical stimulation for pain relief.
summaries.intermediate: In Neural Computation (2019), Arle, Iftimia, Shils, Mei, and Carlson assemble a draft human spinal cord connectome from the literature (cell types, connectivity, and strength indications), filling gaps with other species and estimating neuron counts from cadaveric measurements, histology, and cytoarchitecture. The model covers all ten Rexed laminae across 31 segments with intra- and interlaminar, intersegmental, and brain connections, notes highly recurrent networks, and is applied to spinal cord stimulation for analgesia.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Neuron counts and connection strengths are estimates, often borrowed across species. The abstract does not report simulation parameters or analgesia outcomes. The authors themselves call the model a starting point that requires further calibration.

plain_language_summary: Most wiring maps are of the brain, not the spinal cord. This team builds a first-pass computer model of human spinal circuits from published anatomy and uses it to study electrical stimulation for pain relief.

ocar.opportunity: If spinal interneuron-to-motoneuron wiring can be mapped completely in a vertebrate hemisegment, one can test whether orderly motoneuron recruitment is mostly a biophysical property of the motoneurons or a consequence of specific presynaptic connections.
ocar.challenge: It is controversial how much gradual recruitment depends on intrinsic differences among motoneurons versus specific connections from interneurons onto motoneuron subsets.
ocar.action: Svara, Kornfeld, Denk, and Bollmann report in Cell Reports (2018) a serial block-face electron microscopy (SBEM) reconstruction mapping all connections from two interneuron types onto all motoneurons in a larval zebrafish spinal cord hemisegment.
ocar.resolution: Dorsal excitatory ipsilateral interneurons showed specific synaptic connectivity: large, high-force motoneurons received specific input from dorsally located interneurons active only during fast swims. Ventral excitatory ipsilateral interneurons did not show that specificity. Inhibitory commissural-to-motoneuron connectivity lacked a discernible pattern. The authors conclude recruitment depends to a considerable extent on specific connectivity.
ocar.future_work: The abstract does not state a further experimental program; the implied next question is how far this hemisegment wiring pattern generalizes across segments and speeds.

summaries.beginner: Fish swim at different speeds using different motor cells. This team maps connections from two kinds of spinal interneurons onto motoneurons in one half-segment of a larval zebrafish and finds that some wiring is highly specific while other wiring looks unpatterned.
summaries.intermediate: In Cell Reports (2018), Svara, Kornfeld, Denk, and Bollmann use serial block-face EM to map all connections from two interneuron types onto all motoneurons in a larval zebrafish spinal hemisegment. They report specific connectivity from dorsal but not ventral excitatory ipsilateral interneurons, with large motoneurons (active only when strong force is required) receiving specific input from dorsal interneurons active only during fast swims. Inhibitory commissural–motoneuron connectivity lacked a discernible pattern.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. The reconstruction is one hemisegment, not the whole cord. The abstract does not give synapse counts, cell counts, or statistics. 'All connections' and 'all motoneurons' are claims of the abstract, not independently checkable here.

plain_language_summary: Fish swim at different speeds using different motor cells. This team maps connections from two kinds of spinal interneurons onto motoneurons in one half-segment of a larval zebrafish and finds that some wiring is highly specific while other wiring looks unpatterned.

ocar.opportunity: Classic work by Langley and Sperry suggested neurons carry 'individual identification tags' and connect by chemical affinities. Molecularly diverse cell-surface proteins could supply those identities so neurons distinguish partners and wire with laminar, cellular, and subcellular precision.
ocar.challenge: Cell type-specific surface repertoires and extracellular interaction maps are accumulating, but it remains hard to show how that diversity encodes wiring specificity and synaptic diversity in vertebrate circuits. No single cue appears sufficient, and lock-and-key matching with target cells is often not what the data show.
ocar.action: Joris de Wit and Anirvan Ghosh review in Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2015) the cadherin, neurexin, immunoglobulin, and leucine-rich repeat (LRR) superfamilies as candidate surface codes for specifying connectivity.
ocar.resolution: They argue these families can act in concert during circuit assembly. The strongest in vivo case they highlight is type II cadherins CDH8 and CDH9 instructing laminar choice of bipolar-cell axons in the retina, via heterophilic ligands in the lamina rather than Sperry-style lock-and-key matching with target cells. Neurexin diversity does not appear to encode cellular specificity. Combinatorial coding—many molecules reused across assembly steps—is the emerging picture.
ocar.future_work: The authors call for testing how combinations of surface molecules collaborate at specific synapse types in intact circuits; how activity dynamically alters surface repertoires and synaptic interaction networks in vivo; bridging cell-type expression and interactome maps with functional tests; and exploiting disease-linked surface proteins as drug targets.

summaries.beginner: Brain cells have to pick the right partners to wire up. This review looks at families of sticky surface proteins that may act like name tags, and concludes that many tags working together, not one master code, probably build circuits.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2015), Joris de Wit and Anirvan Ghosh review cadherin, neurexin, immunoglobulin, and leucine-rich-repeat surface proteins as candidate wiring codes. They distinguish laminar, cellular, and subcellular specificity plus synaptic diversity, tracing the idea to Langley and Sperry. They argue the strongest in vivo case is type II cadherins CDH8 and CDH9 biasing bipolar-cell laminar choice in retina via unknown heterophilic ligands, not lock-and-key matching. Combinatorial coding is presented as the working model.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not new experiments. The PDF extract truncates the mid-paper catalog of families (marked [...]) but captures the abstract, opening framework, and Conclusions and perspectives. CDH8/CDH9 evidence is described as 'probably strongest' among cited cases, not as a quantitative reconstruction. Neurexin cellular-specificity claims are qualified (a subcellular role is not ruled out). No sample sizes or accuracies are reported.

plain_language_summary: Brain cells have to pick the right partners to wire up. This review looks at families of sticky surface proteins that may act like name tags, and concludes that many tags working together, not one master code, probably build circuits.

ocar.opportunity: High-resolution electron microscopy can stream petascale anisotropic volumes faster than a finished 3D multi-resolution model can be built. A visualization system that keeps up with that stream would let neuroscientists explore data as it is acquired.
ocar.challenge: Building a full 3D hierarchy (for example an octree) up front does not scale to dense petascale streams, and sample access during ray-casting must not grow with hierarchy size. Missing tiles are the normal case, not an error.
ocar.action: Hadwiger, Beyer, Jeong, and Pfister present in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (2012) a visualization-driven virtual-memory architecture that accepts a constant stream of 2D microscope tiles, treats missing data as cache misses during ray-casting, and constructs 3D blocks from tiles only when they are actually viewed.
ocar.resolution: The design decouples multi-resolution construction from acquisition and decouples sample-access time from hierarchy size, without precomputing a 3D multi-resolution representation. The authors evaluate design choices for scalability and performance against prior systems and illustrate the approach on real neuroscience microscopy data.
ocar.future_work: The abstract does not list a further-work program beyond demonstrating effectiveness on real microscopy streams; generalization to other modalities is not specified here.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes can stream more pictures than a computer can store as a finished 3D model. This system lets scientists fly through the volume while it is still being collected, building 3D chunks only for the parts they are looking at.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (2012), Hadwiger, Beyer, Jeong, and Pfister present a visualization-driven virtual-memory architecture for petascale anisotropic EM streams. It decouples multi-resolution construction from acquisition and sample access from hierarchy size, accepts a constant stream of 2D tiles, does not precompute an octree, and constructs 3D blocks on demand from ray-casting cache misses. They evaluate scalability versus prior systems on real neuroscience microscopy data.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. The abstract claims a first petascale streaming visualization system and an extensive evaluation but does not report timings, dataset sizes, or hardware. Comparison systems are unnamed here.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes can stream more pictures than a computer can store as a finished 3D model. This system lets scientists fly through the volume while it is still being collected, building 3D chunks only for the parts they are looking at.

ocar.opportunity: The newly proposed 'connectome' names a highly organized connection matrix of the human brain. Combining macro- and microscopic data into a statistical ultrastructural model—a 'synaptome'—could make synaptic-level description tractable even if a complete synapse-by-synapse diagram is not.
ocar.challenge: Deciphering how information flows through that matrix is so hard that it may not be achieved soon, if ever. Circuit diagrams at the synaptic level are described as surely impossible to complete.
ocar.action: J. DeFelipe writes in Science (2010) a perspective on moving from connectome language to a synaptome: a realistic statistical model of connectivity at the ultrastructural level.
ocar.resolution: He argues that marrying macro- and microscopic data may still justify optimism even if synaptic completeness is out of reach. The piece is conceptual rather than a new map.
ocar.future_work: The implied next step is advances in combining macro- and microscopic data into a statistical synaptome model; no specific dataset or method is named.

summaries.beginner: Mapping every synapse in a human brain looks nearly impossible. This essay still argues we can be optimistic if we combine large-scale maps with statistics of synapses, a 'synaptome.'
summaries.intermediate: In Science (2010), J. DeFelipe discusses the then-new term 'connectome' as the human brain's connection matrix and the difficulty of tracing information flow, especially at synaptic completeness. He proposes marrying macro- and microscopic data into a realistic statistical ultrastructural model, the 'synaptome.'
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. This is a perspective, not a dataset or method paper. No measurements, reconstructions, or quantitative predictions are given.

plain_language_summary: Mapping every synapse in a human brain looks nearly impossible. This essay still argues we can be optimistic if we combine large-scale maps with statistics of synapses, a 'synaptome.'

ocar.opportunity: Synapse-resolution fruit-fly connectomes across developmental stages make it possible to test how connection probability depends on physical distance, and whether that geometric rule has functional meaning for communication and network criticality.
ocar.challenge: Coarse-grained brain networks had been described with an exponential distance rule. If synapse-resolution data follow a different law, geometry–topology links drawn from coarser maps may not transfer.
ocar.action: Zhang, Moore, Ru, and Yan report in Physical Review Letters (2024) a power-law scaling of neuronal connection probability with spatial distance in fruit-fly synapse-resolution connectomes, plus a connectivity predictor using only interneuronal distance and in- and out-degrees.
ocar.resolution: They find a consistent geometric scaling law across developmental stages, distinct from the exponential distance rule. They argue it aligns with maximum entropy of information communication and a criticality balance of integration and segregation, and that perturbing the empirical model's parameters or type loses those properties.
ocar.future_work: The abstract frames a direct geometry–topology link as an aid to understanding optimal operation in confined space; tests beyond the fly volumes used here are not specified.

summaries.beginner: Nearby neurons are more likely to connect, but the exact rule matters. In fruit-fly wiring maps, connection chance falls with distance as a power law, not the exponential rule seen in coarser brain maps, and that shape appears to keep information flow efficient.
summaries.intermediate: In Physical Review Letters (2024), Zhang, Moore, Ru, and Yan report a power-law scaling of neuronal connection probability with spatial distance in synapse-resolution fruit-fly connectomes across developmental stages, unlike the exponential distance rule of coarse-grained networks. They argue the law aligns with maximum entropy of communication and a criticality balance of integration and segregation, lost under parameter or model-type perturbation. They also derive a connectivity predictor from distance plus in- and out-degrees.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. The abstract does not name which fly datasets, give exponents, sample sizes, or statistical tests. 'Functional significance' is argued via perturbation of a probability model, not a causal experiment, and those analyses are not in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Nearby neurons are more likely to connect, but the exact rule matters. In fruit-fly wiring maps, connection chance falls with distance as a power law, not the exponential rule seen in coarser brain maps, and that shape appears to keep information flow efficient.

ocar.opportunity: Volume electron microscopy now generates large raw volumes that life-science labs need to segment, spatially analyze, and visualize in 3D without a dedicated compute cluster or heavy manual annotation.
ocar.challenge: Users with modest computational expertise need organelle-specific labels, spatial interaction analysis, and rendering, while bridging compatibility among free open-source tools that were not designed as one pipeline.
ocar.action: Müller, Schmidt, Albrecht, Rieckert, Otto, Galicia Garcia, Fabig, Solimena, and Weigert describe in Nature Protocols (2024) an annotation-efficient pipeline using Microscopy Image Browser, ilastik, Labkit, and Album-packaged Python tools (CSBDeep, CellSketch, StarDist, Blender, Jupyter notebooks) that can run on a single standard workstation.
ocar.resolution: The protocol covers raw-data preparation, organelle-specific segmentation, spatial analysis, and 3D visualization, with guidelines for choosing tools per organelle. Album solutions are distributed to ease installation and glue steps together.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the description as a reference for similar single- or multiple-organelle projects on single-user setups; new algorithms are not claimed.

summaries.beginner: Volume electron microscopy produces huge 3D cell pictures, but drawing every organelle by hand is exhausting. This protocol walks biologists through free tools that can label organelles, measure how they sit next to each other, and render them in 3D on an ordinary workstation.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Protocols (2024), Müller, Schmidt, Albrecht, Rieckert, Otto, Galicia Garcia, Fabig, Solimena, and Weigert describe an annotation-efficient pipeline for organelle segmentation, spatial analysis, and 3D visualization of volume-EM datasets using Microscopy Image Browser, ilastik, Labkit, and Album-packaged Python tools (CSBDeep, CellSketch, StarDist, Blender, Jupyter). It is aimed at life-science users with modest computational expertise on a single workstation.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. This is a protocol, not a benchmarked accuracy study; no Dice scores, dataset sizes, or timing numbers appear in the abstract. Tool choice is described as organelle-dependent without a decision table here.

plain_language_summary: Volume electron microscopy produces huge 3D cell pictures, but drawing every organelle by hand is exhausting. This protocol walks biologists through free tools that can label organelles, measure how they sit next to each other, and render them in 3D on an ordinary workstation.

ocar.opportunity: Stroke is a leading cause of adult disability, and recovery involves remapping of complex brain networks. Graph-theoretic connectomics across scales could better evaluate structural and functional reorganization after stroke.
ocar.challenge: Macroscale effects of stroke on brain networks are increasingly characterized, but reorganization of smaller-scale networks remains incompletely understood. Damage and recovery span many spatiotemporal scales at once.
ocar.action: Latifi and Carmichael review in Trends in Neurosciences (2024) stroke-related connectivity studies using a graph-theory frame from nano- to macroscales, arguing for multiscale connectomics-based approaches.
ocar.resolution: They conclude that looking across scales may provide new routes to evaluate structural and functional remapping after stroke and during recovery. The paper is a review, not a new cohort study.
ocar.future_work: The implied program is applying multiscale connectomics to better evaluate remapping during recovery; specific trials or datasets are not named in the abstract.

summaries.beginner: Stroke recovery is not just a hole in one brain region; networks reorganize at many size scales. This review uses network language to argue that looking across those scales could better explain how brains remap after a stroke.
summaries.intermediate: In Trends in Neurosciences (2024), Latifi and Carmichael review multiscale connectomics for stroke, using graph theory from nano- to macroscales. They note that macroscale network effects of stroke are better characterized than smaller-scale reorganization, and argue that multiscale approaches may better evaluate structural and functional remapping during recovery.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. This is a review without original patient cohorts, named imaging modalities in detail, or quantitative recovery metrics.

plain_language_summary: Stroke recovery is not just a hole in one brain region; networks reorganize at many size scales. This review uses network language to argue that looking across those scales could better explain how brains remap after a stroke.

ocar.opportunity: The hippocampus is widely connected with cortex, thalamus, hypothalamus, olfactory areas, and amygdala, but how single hippocampal neurons project brain-wide, and how soma location specifies those projectomes, has been unclear.
ocar.challenge: Axon arbors of individual hippocampal neurons had not been reconstructed at this scale, so organization principles linking soma position, transcriptomic subdomain, and whole-brain targets were incomplete.
ocar.action: Qiu, Hu, Huang, Gao, Wang, and colleagues report in Science (2024) reconstruction of 10,100 single-neuron projectomes of mouse hippocampus using sparse labeling and fluorescence micro-optical sectioning tomography, with spatial transcriptomics of hippocampal sections and an open queryable database.
ocar.resolution: Neurons were classified into 341 projection patterns and then 43 projectome subtypes. Number of targets and axon-tip distribution depended on soma location along longitudinal and transverse axes; many subtypes were enriched in transcriptomic HIP subdomains. The authors map intra-HPF versus extra-HPF wiring and report that bihemispheric projecting neurons generally target one homologous pair with ipsilateral preference.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the projectomes as a structural basis for hippocampal function and as combinable with gene expression to define subtypes; synaptic-resolution connectivity is outside this light-microscopic projectome resource.

summaries.beginner: Hippocampal cells send axons across the brain, but maps of those paths have been incomplete. This team traces more than ten thousand individual mouse hippocampal neurons, groups them into dozens of projection types, and shows that where a cell sits predicts where its axon goes.
summaries.intermediate: In Science (2024), Qiu, Hu, Huang, Gao, Wang, and colleagues reconstruct 10,100 single-neuron projectomes of mouse hippocampus using sparse labeling and fluorescence micro-optical sectioning tomography, classifying 43 projectome subtypes from 341 projection patterns. Projection-target number and axon-tip distribution depend on soma location along longitudinal and transverse axes; many subtypes enrich in transcriptomic hippocampal subdomains. They map intra- versus extra-hippocampal-formation wiring and report that bihemispheric neurons generally project to one homologous pair with ipsilateral preference.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Counts 10,100 / 43 / 341 are abstract claims, not checkable against figures here. Spatial transcriptomics is correlated with soma location, not a causal mapping. Imaging is light-microscopic projectomes, not synaptic EM.

plain_language_summary: Hippocampal cells send axons across the brain, but maps of those paths have been incomplete. This team traces more than ten thousand individual mouse hippocampal neurons, groups them into dozens of projection types, and shows that where a cell sits predicts where its axon goes.

ocar.opportunity: Papilio xuthus has six spectral photoreceptor classes and three ommatidium types and can detect 1 nm wavelength differences from ultraviolet to red. A lamina connectome could explain that precision and enable circuit-level comparison with Drosophila, whose color vision is more limited.
ocar.challenge: Connectomics of early wavelength processing has focused on Drosophila. How a richer photoreceptor palette is wired in the first optic ganglion, including possible inter-photoreceptor and inter-cartridge links, was unknown.
ocar.action: Matsushita, Stewart, Ilić, Chen, Wakita, Miyazaki, Murata, Kinoshita, Belušič, and Arikawa report in Current Biology (2022) a connectome analysis of the lamina of Papilio xuthus.
ocar.resolution: Cartridges typically contain nine photoreceptor axons from one ommatidium and four second-order neurons. The authors found abundant inter-photoreceptor connections, which are absent in the Drosophila lamina, and connections between neighboring cartridges, especially those from spectrally distinct ommatidia. Linear summation of synaptic connections is said to explain spectral sensitivity of photoreceptors and second-order neurons in the lamina.
ocar.future_work: The introduction frames comparative circuit studies as the route to asking how precise color vision evolves; further ganglia are not mapped here.

summaries.beginner: Butterflies see color more finely than fruit flies, with six kinds of light sensors packed in three ommatidium types. Mapping the first visual station of a swallowtail shows photoreceptors talking to each other and to neighboring cartridges, which can explain their spectral tuning.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology (2022), Matsushita, Stewart, Ilić, Chen, Wakita, Miyazaki, Murata, Kinoshita, Belušič, and Arikawa reconstruct the lamina of Papilio xuthus. Cartridges typically contain nine photoreceptor axons and four second-order neurons. They report abundant inter-photoreceptor connections absent in the Drosophila lamina, plus inter-cartridge links especially between spectrally distinct ommatidia. Linear summation of synaptic connections is said to explain spectral sensitivity of photoreceptors and second-order neurons.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. No synapse counts, number of cartridges reconstructed, or goodness-of-fit for the linear-summation model are given. Comparison to Drosophila is qualitative in the abstract. The 1 nm behavioral discrimination is cited as background, not a result of this reconstruction.

plain_language_summary: Butterflies see color more finely than fruit flies, with six kinds of light sensors packed in three ommatidium types. Mapping the first visual station of a swallowtail shows photoreceptors talking to each other and to neighboring cartridges, which can explain their spectral tuning.

ocar.opportunity: Deeper layers of the auditory system have not been fully mapped in any model system. Linking a comprehensive wiring diagram of Drosophila song-perception circuits to physiological response profiles would close that gap at synaptic resolution.
ocar.challenge: Without both complete connectivity and response profiles, it is hard to explain how song is processed beyond the earliest auditory stations.
ocar.action: Bates and Jefferis write in Current Biology (2022) a dispatch highlighting a new study that links comprehensive connectomics of Drosophila song-perception circuits to physiological response profiles.
ocar.resolution: The dispatch's contribution is to flag that combination of complete wiring and physiology, not to present a new reconstruction of its own.
ocar.future_work: The abstract does not outline further experiments beyond noting that deeper auditory layers had not been fully mapped.

summaries.beginner: Scientists still lack a full map of how flies hear song in deeper brain layers. This short commentary highlights a new study that pairs a wiring map of those circuits with how the cells actually respond to sound.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Biology (2022), A. S. Bates and G. Jefferis write a dispatch noting that deeper auditory layers have not been fully mapped in any model system, and highlighting a new study that links comprehensive Drosophila song-perception connectomics to physiological response profiles.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. This is a commentary, not the primary reconstruction. The abstract does not name the highlighted paper's authors, neuron counts, or physiological findings, so those results must not be inferred here.

plain_language_summary: Scientists still lack a full map of how flies hear song in deeper brain layers. This short commentary highlights a new study that pairs a wiring map of those circuits with how the cells actually respond to sound.

ocar.opportunity: If neural activity during development sculpts fly circuits as well as mammalian ones, Drosophila's genetic toolkit could be used to learn general rules of activity-dependent brain assembly.
ocar.challenge: Fly wiring was widely thought to be specified by genetically hardwired cell-recognition molecules, sufficient to determine the connectome without a developmental activity requirement.
ocar.action: Akin and Zipursky review in Current Opinion in Genetics and Development (2020) recent findings that activity during development also contributes to circuit assembly in Drosophila.
ocar.resolution: They argue that activity is a fundamental aspect of brain development in general, and that fly tools for circuit development, structure, and function offer a route to study it.
ocar.future_work: The abstract highlights opportunities to learn about activity-dependent assembly through Drosophila methods; specific circuits or manipulations are not listed here.

summaries.beginner: Fly brains were thought to wire themselves using only molecular name tags, unlike mammals where neural activity also sculpts circuits. This review collects recent evidence that activity during development also helps assemble fly circuits.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Genetics and Development (2020), Akin and Zipursky review evidence that developmental activity contributes to Drosophila circuit assembly, contrary to a view that genetically hardwired cell-recognition molecules suffice to specify the connectome. They suggest activity is a general feature of brain development and that fly genetic tools can dissect it.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. No specific circuits, activity manipulations, or quantitative results are named. This is an opinion/review, not new data.

plain_language_summary: Fly brains were thought to wire themselves using only molecular name tags, unlike mammals where neural activity also sculpts circuits. This review collects recent evidence that activity during development also helps assemble fly circuits.

ocar.opportunity: Thalamocortical synapses are well studied in primary sensory cortex, but much less is known about higher-order thalamic projections into higher-order cortical areas, which likely form a majority of thalamocortical circuitry.
ocar.challenge: Labeling must mark thalamocortical axons and synapses without retrograde contamination, across cortical layers, at ultrastructural resolution.
ocar.action: Sampathkumar, Miller-Hansen, Sherman, and Kasthuri report in the European Journal of Neuroscience (2020) an intersectional viral approach (cre plus cre-dependent ascorbate peroxidase) labeling posterior medial nucleus axons into mouse secondary somatosensory cortex, reconstructed with large-volume serial electron microscopy.
ocar.resolution: Labeled thalamocortical synapses were 14% of all synapses in the cortical volume, matching previous estimates of first-order thalamocortical input fraction. Relative to unlabeled terminals, labeled ones were larger, more often contained a mitochondrion, more often targeted spiny (not aspiny) dendrites, and often innervated larger spines with spine apparatuses. Labeled terminals were more prevalent in layers 2/3, and labeled-versus-unlabeled differences were greatest there, contrasting first-order reports of larger labeled terminals in layer 4 than layers 2/3.
ocar.future_work: The authors point to the need for more analyses of higher-order thalamocortical ultrastructure, which they suggest represents a majority of thalamocortical circuitry.

summaries.beginner: Most synapse-level maps of thalamic input come from primary sensory cortex. This team labels axons from a higher-order thalamic nucleus into mouse secondary somatosensory cortex and finds those synapses look larger and more spine-preferring than unlabeled ones, especially in upper layers.
summaries.intermediate: In the European Journal of Neuroscience (2020), Sampathkumar, Miller-Hansen, Sherman, and Kasthuri combine cre-dependent ascorbate peroxidase labeling of posterior medial nucleus axons with serial EM in mouse secondary somatosensory cortex. Labeled thalamocortical synapses were 14% of synapses in the volume. Relative to unlabeled terminals, labeled ones were larger, more often mitochondrial, more spine-targeting, and often innervated larger spines with spine apparatuses; differences were greatest in layers 2/3, contrasting first-order patterns where labeled terminals were larger in layer 4 than layers 2/3.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. The 14% figure and qualitative ultrastructural differences are abstract-level; numbers of terminals, volume size, and statistics are not given. One mouse pathway (posterior medial nucleus to S2) is the case study.

plain_language_summary: Most synapse-level maps of thalamic input come from primary sensory cortex. This team labels axons from a higher-order thalamic nucleus into mouse secondary somatosensory cortex and finds those synapses look larger and more spine-preferring than unlabeled ones, especially in upper layers.

ocar.opportunity: Each whisker maps to an anatomical 'barrel' in rodent somatosensory cortex, so tactile computations can be studied inside a well-defined map. Linking cell-type-specific connectivity to activity during whisker behaviors could explain sensory-guided decisions.
ocar.challenge: Excitatory and inhibitory classes must be defined by anatomy, physiology, and molecules; local microcircuits, long-range interactions, and neuromodulation are only beginning to be understood together with behavior.
ocar.action: Staiger and Petersen review in Physiological Reviews (2020) signaling pathways from whiskers to barrel cortex (wS1), cell types, synaptic connectivity, neuromodulators, and cell-type-specific activity during whisker-related behaviors.
ocar.resolution: The review synthesizes current understanding of wS1 microcircuits and long-range interactions and frames an agenda for causal, mechanistic accounts of which tactile features are processed by which cell types and sent downstream.
ocar.future_work: The authors state an important goal: causal and mechanistic understanding of how selected tactile information is processed by specific neuron types in synaptically connected wS1 networks and signaled to downstream areas for sensory-guided decision-making.

summaries.beginner: Each whisker on a rodent's snout has its own patch of cortex, called a barrel. This long review walks through how signals get there, what cell types live in a barrel, and how those cells work together when the animal uses its whiskers.
summaries.intermediate: In Physiological Reviews (2020), Staiger and Petersen review whisker pathways to barrel cortex (wS1), excitatory and inhibitory cell classes defined anatomically, electrophysiologically, and molecularly, local and long-range connectivity, neuromodulation, and links from cell-type-specific connectivity to activity during whisker behaviors. They frame a future goal of causal, mechanistic accounts of tactile computations signaled to downstream areas for decision-making.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. This is a broad review without original sample sizes or a single new circuit map. Cell-type catalogs and connectivity are described as beginning to be understood.

plain_language_summary: Each whisker on a rodent's snout has its own patch of cortex, called a barrel. This long review walks through how signals get there, what cell types live in a barrel, and how those cells work together when the animal uses its whiskers.

ocar.opportunity: Three-dimensional and large-field scanning electron microscopy is limited by acquisition time, and biological tissue is sensitive to electron dose. Random sparse scanning plus reconstruction could cut dwell time while still supporting automated neuron segmentation.
ocar.challenge: Missing pixels must be filled well enough that deep-learning segmentation of neurons remains usable, and the workflow must run on a real microscope, not only simulated sparse data.
ocar.action: Potocek, Trampert, Peemen, Schoenmakers, and Dahmen report in Microscopy and Microanalysis (2020) a workflow of sparse SEM acquisition, reconstruction by compressive sensing or neural networks, and deep-learning neuron segmentation.
ocar.resolution: They report that average dwell time per pixel can be reduced by a factor of 2–3, described as real-life confirmation of previous simulated-data results in a key connectomics segmentation application, demonstrating feasibility of random sparse scanning in that scenario.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents feasibility for this segmentation setting; broader dose/time gains on other tissues or tasks are not claimed here.

summaries.beginner: Taking electron-microscope pictures of brain tissue is slow and can damage the sample. This team scans only some pixels at random, fills in the missing bits with reconstruction methods or neural nets, and still automatically traces neurons.
summaries.intermediate: In Microscopy and Microanalysis (2020), Potocek, Trampert, Peemen, Schoenmakers, and Dahmen demonstrate sparse random scanning on an SEM, reconstruct images with compressive sensing or neural networks, then segment neurons with deep learning. They report average dwell time per pixel reduced by a factor of 2–3, described as real-life confirmation of prior simulated-data results for a key connectomics segmentation application.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. The 2–3× dwell-time factor is the only quantitative claim; dataset identity, segmentation metrics, and reconstruction error are not given. Feasibility is argued for one real-world scenario.

plain_language_summary: Taking electron-microscope pictures of brain tissue is slow and can damage the sample. This team scans only some pixels at random, fills in the missing bits with reconstruction methods or neural nets, and still automatically traces neurons.

ocar.opportunity: At the centenary of D'Arcy Thompson's On Growth and Form, experimental advances allow study of how anatomical brain networks change. Principles of connectome development could inform personalized treatment of developmental brain disease.
ocar.challenge: A developing connectome cannot be observed directly in full: one axon can be watched, but not all cells at once. Linking cognition and behavior to network change requires knowing which spatial and temporal factors produce adult topology.
ocar.action: Marcus Kaiser reviews in Trends in Cognitive Sciences (2017) candidate mechanisms of connectome development, emphasizing how spatial distance and temporal birth time and connection formation shape bidirectional and long-distance connections, modules, and hubs in health and disease.
ocar.resolution: The review argues that adult organization is shaped by those spatial and temporal factors, visible across developmental stages and in computational models at neuronal and fiber-tract levels. A Trends box highlights birth timing, distance, modules, and hubs as organizing themes.
ocar.future_work: The paper's Future Work section calls for connectivity at early stages and same-individual longitudinal data; notes that macroconnectome follow-ups are mostly 1–2 years because longer studies face recruitment, protocol, scanner, and funding limits; that microconnectome data remain largely in vitro (e.g. hippocampal cultures showing rich-club connectivity); and that models need experimentally derived parameters and feasible large-scale simulators (NetMorph, Cx3D, and related efforts). Further undiscovered mechanisms are expected.

summaries.beginner: Brains do not start out looking like adult wiring diagrams. This review asks how space and timing during growth produce the long-range links, hubs, and modules we see later, and why that matters for developmental brain disease.
summaries.intermediate: In Trends in Cognitive Sciences (2017), Marcus Kaiser outlines candidate principles of connectome development, tying the discussion to D'Arcy Thompson's morphology centenary. Spatial distance and temporal birth and connection timing are argued to influence bidirectional and long-distance connections, modules, and hubs. He calls for longitudinal studies, experimentally derived connection-formation parameters, and biologically realistic models, noting Developing Connectome Project in-utero data and rich-club architecture in newborns.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not a new connectome dataset. The PDF extract truncates the mid-paper body (marked [...]) but captures the Trends box, opening argument, and an explicit Future Work section. No original sample sizes or accuracies are claimed. Microconnectome evidence cited in Future Work is in vitro, not whole-brain EM. The Human Brain Project is noted as not modeling network development.

plain_language_summary: Brains do not start out looking like adult wiring diagrams. This review asks how space and timing during growth produce the long-range links, hubs, and modules we see later, and why that matters for developmental brain disease.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics and other neuroanatomy need brain banking that keeps ultrastructure stable for long periods yet still allows high-resolution imaging. A method that scales by perfusion to large brains would widen sample access.
ocar.challenge: Ice formation destroys ultrastructure; purely chemical fixation does not by itself provide indefinite ice-free storage. Cryoprotectant must be loaded and later removed without ruining synapses.
ocar.action: McIntyre and Fahy report in Cryobiology (2015) aldehyde-stabilized cryopreservation (ASC): rabbit and pig brains are glutaraldehyde-perfused, loaded to 65% w/v ethylene glycol, and vitrified at −135 °C, then rewarmed with cryoprotectant removal by perfusion or slice diffusion, and evaluated by EM and FIB-SEM.
ocar.resolution: The authors report uniformly excellent preservation: processes easily traceable and synapses crisp in both species across multiple regions and selected FIB-SEM volumes. They highlight perfusion scalability, vitrified long-term storage, and a perfusable aldehyde-preserved brain after cryoprotectant removal.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents ASC as enabling scaled brain banking for assays including connectomics; human brains and quantitative segmentation benchmarks are not reported here.

summaries.beginner: Brains for wiring studies need to stay well preserved for a long time. This method first chemically fixes rabbit and pig brains, then fills them with antifreeze so they can be stored glassy-cold without ice, and later warmed for electron microscopy.
summaries.intermediate: In Cryobiology (2015), McIntyre and Fahy introduce aldehyde-stabilized cryopreservation: rabbit and pig brains are glutaraldehyde-perfused, slowly loaded to 65% w/v ethylene glycol, and vitrified at −135 °C. After rewarming and cryoprotectant removal, EM and FIB-SEM across regions showed uniformly excellent preservation with traceable processes and crisp synapses. They highlight perfusion scalability, ice-free long-term storage, and a perfusable aldehyde-preserved brain after cryoprotectant removal.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. 'Uniformly excellent' is qualitative; no synapse-detection scores, volume sizes, or counts of sampled regions are given. Species are rabbit and pig, not human.

plain_language_summary: Brains for wiring studies need to stay well preserved for a long time. This method first chemically fixes rabbit and pig brains, then fills them with antifreeze so they can be stored glassy-cold without ice, and later warmed for electron microscopy.

ocar.opportunity: Visual motion detection is a classic neural-computation problem. A complete EM wiring diagram of the relevant fly visual neurons, with precise synaptic counts, could identify the circuit that actually computes motion.
ocar.challenge: Understanding had been frustrated by incomplete knowledge of the relevant neurons and synapses. Light microscopy only estimates connections from arbor overlap.
ocar.action: Shin-ya Takemura reviews in Microscopy (2015) connectomic studies of Drosophila visual circuitry, emphasizing comprehensive EM reconstruction of the motion-computation circuit.
ocar.resolution: The review states that connectomic studies successfully identified the concrete neuronal circuit in the fly visual system that computes motion signals, aided by EM's unequivocal connections and precise synaptic counts compared with light microscopy. Connectomes are framed as a foundation for linking circuits to function.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents connectomes as a foundation for understanding neuronal function by identifying underlying circuits; further specific experiments are not listed.

summaries.beginner: How flies see motion was a famous unsolved wiring problem. Electron-microscope maps of the fruit-fly visual system identified the actual circuit that computes motion, with counted synapses rather than guessed contacts.
summaries.intermediate: In Microscopy (2015), Shin-ya Takemura reviews EM connectomics of Drosophila visual circuitry, emphasizing that comprehensive reconstruction identified the neuronal circuit computing motion signals. EM is contrasted with light microscopy: unequivocal connections and precise synaptic counts versus estimated overlap. The review frames connectomes as a foundation for linking circuits to function.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. This is a review of prior reconstructions, not a new volume. Circuit names, synapse counts, and completeness metrics are not in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: How flies see motion was a famous unsolved wiring problem. Electron-microscope maps of the fruit-fly visual system identified the actual circuit that computes motion, with counted synapses rather than guessed contacts.

ocar.opportunity: Serial ultrastructural observation with scanning electron microscopy, plus heavy-metal staining for SEM contrast, has opened a path toward complete neuronal connection maps—connectomes—in the central nervous system.
ocar.challenge: Methods differ in resolution, imaging speed, target size, and whether re-observation is possible, so they must be chosen to match the question. Huge datasets remain a major obstacle without automated segmentation and 3D reconstruction.
ocar.action: Ohno, Katoh, Saitoh, Saitoh, and Ohno review in Microscopy (2015) three-dimensional volume imaging with electron microscopy toward connectome, contrasting serial SEM with conventional serial-section TEM and discussing tissue preparation that increases heavy-metal deposition.
ocar.resolution: They argue advanced SEM methods should be selected by target tissue size, required spatial resolution, and need for re-observation, and that automation in segmentation and 3D reconstruction will be critical for larger brain volumes.
ocar.future_work: The authors await future improvements in acquisition and analysis of morphological data to relate whole connectome structure to consciousness, intelligence, and memory—an aspirational framing, not a demonstrated result.

summaries.beginner: Classic electron microscopy looks at thin slices one at a time. New scanning-EM methods can stack many slices into a 3D volume, which is how researchers hope to reconstruct brain wiring, though huge datasets still need better automatic tracing.
summaries.intermediate: In Microscopy (2015), Ohno, Katoh, Saitoh, Saitoh, and Ohno review serial SEM volume imaging for connectomics, contrasting it with serial-section TEM, and discuss tissue preparation that increases heavy-metal deposition for SEM. They note method-specific tradeoffs in resolution, speed, re-observation, and target size, and flag automation of segmentation and 3D reconstruction as critical for larger volumes.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. No particular SEM platform (SBF-SEM, FIB-SEM, ATUM) is named, and no performance numbers are given. Closing remarks on consciousness, intelligence, and memory are speculative framing, not results.

plain_language_summary: Classic electron microscopy looks at thin slices one at a time. New scanning-EM methods can stack many slices into a 3D volume, which is how researchers hope to reconstruct brain wiring, though huge datasets still need better automatic tracing.

ocar.opportunity: Cosmology already solved querying skies too large for a workstation, via data-center computing (Sloan Digital Sky Survey). The same model could shorten idea-to-discovery time in connectomics at the Open Connectome Project.
ocar.challenge: In data-intensive science, scale and complexity exceed local stores. Different computing models are optimized for different data, and remote users must query subsets efficiently.
ocar.action: Burns, Vogelstein, and Szalay write in Neuron (2014) about how data-intensive systems originally built for SDSS are used in connectomics at the Open Connectome Project, listing lessons learned and outlining expected challenges.
ocar.resolution: They argue cloud computing, using data centers and high-performance clusters, is the preeminent model, and that success in computational connectomics would drastically reduce time between idea and discovery, as SDSS did in cosmology.
ocar.future_work: The abstract says they outline the top challenges they expect to face; those challenges are not enumerated in the abstract itself.

summaries.beginner: Astronomy already learned to store and query skies too big for a laptop. This essay describes how the same kind of data-center computing, first built for the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, is being reused for brain wiring maps.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron (2014), Burns, Vogelstein, and Szalay argue that data-intensive science outgrows local workstations, making cloud and data-center computing the default. They examine how SDSS-style systems are used at the Open Connectome Project, list lessons learned, and outline expected challenges, hoping computational connectomics will shorten idea-to-discovery time as SDSS did in cosmology.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Lessons and challenges are not enumerated here. No dataset sizes, query benchmarks, or architecture diagrams appear.

plain_language_summary: Astronomy already learned to store and query skies too big for a laptop. This essay describes how the same kind of data-center computing, first built for the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, is being reused for brain wiring maps.

ocar.opportunity: If brain connectivity is abstracted to a graph of neural elements (nodes) and structural, functional, or causal interactions (edges), graph theory offers a rich toolkit for anatomical and dynamical properties of the human connectome.
ocar.challenge: Rapid uptake in neuroimaging brings pitfalls and unresolved challenges that, without caution, can undermine explanatory power.
ocar.action: Fornito, Zalesky, and Breakspear review in NeuroImage (2013) graph analysis of the human connectome, covering promise, progress, pitfalls, prevailing solutions, and frontier challenges.
ocar.resolution: The review organizes how connectomic data enter graph theory and warns that the approach's potential depends on handling those pitfalls. It is a conceptual survey, not a new network map.
ocar.future_work: The authors point to challenges at the forefront of the field; specific remaining problems are not listed in the abstract.

summaries.beginner: Treating the brain as a network of dots and lines lets scientists borrow math from graph theory. This review celebrates that approach for human brain maps but warns about mistakes that can make the results misleading.
summaries.intermediate: In NeuroImage (2013), Fornito, Zalesky, and Breakspear review graph analysis of the human connectome: nodes as neural elements, edges as structural, functional, or causal interactions. They survey rapid uptake in neuroimaging, then focus on pitfalls, prevailing solutions, and frontier challenges that can undermine explanation if ignored.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Specific pitfalls (for example parcellation or thresholding) are not listed. This is a conceptual review without original graph metrics.

plain_language_summary: Treating the brain as a network of dots and lines lets scientists borrow math from graph theory. This review celebrates that approach for human brain maps but warns about mistakes that can make the results misleading.

ocar.opportunity: A complete wiring diagram offers an alternative to conventional circuit analysis, but only if neuronal processes can be segmented and traced through the large image sets from optical or electron microscopy.
ocar.challenge: Tracing is a major obstacle. Novel optical imaging techniques also pose new image-analysis problems for automated algorithms.
ocar.action: Ju Lu reviews in Neuroinformatics (2011) recent progress in automated tracing algorithms for connectomic reconstruction with fluorescence and electron microscopy, and discusses challenges from novel optical methods.
ocar.resolution: The review surveys automated tracing progress and the new difficulties optical techniques introduce. It does not present a new tracer of its own.
ocar.future_work: Challenges to image analysis from novel optical imaging are highlighted as open; specific benchmarks are not given.

summaries.beginner: The hard part of a wiring diagram is following every branch through a mountain of microscope pictures. This review covers computer programs that try to trace neurons automatically in fluorescence and electron-microscope images, and the new headaches created by novel optical methods.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuroinformatics (2011), Ju Lu reviews automated tracing algorithms for connectomic reconstruction from fluorescence and electron microscopy, and discusses image-analysis challenges posed by novel optical imaging techniques.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. No algorithm names, error rates, or dataset comparisons are given. Scope is a review of progress, not a new tracer.

plain_language_summary: The hard part of a wiring diagram is following every branch through a mountain of microscope pictures. This review covers computer programs that try to trace neurons automatically in fluorescence and electron-microscope images, and the new headaches created by novel optical methods.

ocar.opportunity: Complete connectivity reconstructions (connectomics) need maps with high resolution that can be acquired and analyzed faster than serial EM of an entire circuit. Sampling synapses with fluorescent markers and reconstructing statistically could cut that cost.
ocar.challenge: Physical organization of nervous systems remains incompletely known. Full EM reconstructions are slow; any alternative must be robust to errors and still yield high-resolution connectivity.
ocar.action: Y. Mishchenko proposes in Journal of Neuroscience Methods (2011) sampling connectivity with anatomical fluorescent synaptic markers localized by randomized genetic targeting, then reconstructing the connectivity matrix statistically with compressive sensing, tested in simulations on the C. elegans EM wiring diagram.
ocar.resolution: Simulations suggest that diagram could in principle be re-obtained in 1–7 days of imaging and data analysis, versus at least 1–2 years for alternative approaches then available. Compressive sensing is presented as the key to accurate reconstructions from orders-of-magnitude less data. Applications to larger organisms such as Drosophila are discussed.
ocar.future_work: Possible applications in larger organisms such as Drosophila are discussed; they are not demonstrated.

summaries.beginner: Fully mapping a nervous system with electron microscopy is slow. This paper proposes randomly tagging synapses with fluorescent markers and reconstructing the wiring statistically, and simulations suggest the worm's known diagram could be recovered in days rather than years.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Neuroscience Methods (2011), Y. Mishchenko proposes sampling physical connectivity with anatomical fluorescent synaptic markers plus randomized genetic targeting, then reconstructing the connectivity matrix with compressive sensing. Simulations on the C. elegans EM wiring diagram suggest reconstruction in 1–7 days of imaging and analysis versus at least 1–2 years for alternative approaches at the time. Applications to larger organisms such as Drosophila are discussed.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. The 1–7 day and 1–2 year figures come from simulations, not a wet-lab reconstruction. Marker chemistry, targeting efficiency, and empirical error rates are not reported. Drosophila application is prospective.

plain_language_summary: Fully mapping a nervous system with electron microscopy is slow. This paper proposes randomly tagging synapses with fluorescent markers and reconstructing the wiring statistically, and simulations suggest the worm's known diagram could be recovered in days rather than years.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans has a comprehensive synaptic wiring diagram and emerging neuron-specific gene-expression profiles, making it possible to ask which genes jointly predict who connects to whom.
ocar.challenge: Linking those two data types computationally requires identifying synergistic gene sets, not just single genes, whose combined expression predicts connectivity.
ocar.action: Varadan, Miller, and Anastassiou present in Intelligent Systems in Molecular Biology (2006) Entropy Minimization and Boolean Parsimony (EMBP), plus an information-theoretic multivariate synergy measure, applied to publicly available C. elegans data.
ocar.resolution: They report gene sets whose joint expression predicts neural connectivity and whose synergy is exceptionally high, suggesting joint pathway involvement. They describe the results as preliminary and the strategy as one that should improve as more neuron-specific expression data emerge.
ocar.future_work: The authors expect more accurate results as neuron-specific gene-expression data grow, ultimately aiming at clues to universal mechanisms of neural interconnectivity.

summaries.beginner: The worm's wiring diagram is known, and gene activity in individual neurons is becoming known. This computational method looks for groups of genes whose combined on/off pattern predicts which neurons synapse, suggesting they work together.
summaries.intermediate: In Intelligent Systems in Molecular Biology (2006), Varadan, Miller, and Anastassiou present Entropy Minimization and Boolean Parsimony (EMBP) to find synergistically interacting gene sets whose joint expression predicts C. elegans neural connectivity. They introduce an information-theoretic multivariate synergy measure, report that identified sets show exceptionally high synergy suggesting joint pathway involvement, and validate preliminary results on publicly available data.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. Gene-set identities, synergy values, and validation details are not given. Authors describe results as preliminary and expected to improve with more neuron-specific expression data.

plain_language_summary: The worm's wiring diagram is known, and gene activity in individual neurons is becoming known. This computational method looks for groups of genes whose combined on/off pattern predicts which neurons synapse, suggesting they work together.

ocar.opportunity: The midget–parvocellular pathway supports high-acuity vision. Comparing OFF midget bipolar output synapses in dichromatic and trichromatic marmosets and in macaque tests whether this 1:1 midget circuitry depends on trichromatic color vision.
ocar.challenge: Output synapse numbers had to be counted with consistent markers across species and color-vision genotypes in central retina.
ocar.action: Jusuf, Martin, and Grünert report in The Journal of Comparative Neurology (2006) immunocytochemical identification of OFF midget bipolar output synapses (ribbon proteins or GluR4) in Callithrix jacchus (dichromatic and trichromatic) and Macaca fascicularis, with marmoset midget ganglion cells retrogradely labeled from parvocellular LGN.
ocar.resolution: Marmoset midget bipolar cells contacted midget ganglion cells at 1:1, consistent with Old World primates. Output synapses per OFF midget bipolar axon terminal: dichromatic marmoset, 104 cells, range 10–71, mean 29.7 ± 12.4 SD; trichromatic marmoset, 108 cells, 12–86, 28.6 ± 11.7; macaque, 118 cells, 9–48, 26.5 ± 9.3. Distributions were unimodal. The authors conclude midget circuitry is comparable in dichromatic and trichromatic animals.
ocar.future_work: The abstract does not state a further experimental program beyond the comparative conclusion.

summaries.beginner: In primates, midget bipolar cells usually talk one-to-one with midget ganglion cells, a circuit important for sharp vision. Counting their output synapses in marmosets and macaques, including color-seeing and non-color-seeing marmosets, shows similar numbers, suggesting this wiring does not depend on having full color vision.
summaries.intermediate: In The Journal of Comparative Neurology (2006), Jusuf, Martin, and Grünert study OFF midget bipolar connectivity in central retina of marmoset (dichromatic and trichromatic) and macaque. Midget bipolar–ganglion contacts were 1:1 in marmoset, matching Old World primates. Output synapses per OFF midget bipolar axon terminal averaged 29.7 ± 12.4 (n=104 cells) in dichromatic marmoset, 28.6 ± 11.7 (n=108) in trichromatic marmoset, and 26.5 ± 9.3 (n=118) in macaque, with unimodal distributions. They conclude midget circuitry is comparable across these color-vision types.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. The sample is two dichromatic marmosets, one trichromatic marmoset, and one macaque; the ON pathway is not quantified here. Identification is immunocytochemical (kinesin, CtBP2, GluR4, CD15, recoverin), not EM connectomics.

plain_language_summary: In primates, midget bipolar cells usually talk one-to-one with midget ganglion cells, a circuit important for sharp vision. Counting their output synapses in marmosets and macaques, including color-seeing and non-color-seeing marmosets, shows similar numbers, suggesting this wiring does not depend on having full color vision.

ocar.opportunity: The hippocampal mossy fiber synapse is large enough for direct presynaptic recording, so it can serve as a mammalian counterpart to the squid giant synapse and the calyx of Held for relating synaptic biophysics to network computations such as learning, memory, pattern separation, and pattern completion.
ocar.challenge: The idea that this synapse is a powerful 'teacher' or 'detonator' of CA3 has not been fully tested, and the synaptic mechanisms that would support that role—and roles in recall and higher-order computations—have been unclear.
ocar.action: Vandael and Jonas review in Science (2024) structure, biophysics, and circuit function of the hippocampal mossy fiber terminal, synthesizing presynaptic and paired patch-clamp, super-resolution light microscopy, and freeze-fracture and flash-and-freeze electron microscopy.
ocar.resolution: They link distinctive facilitation to coupling between Ca2+ channels and release sensors, and potentiation to vesicle-pool size and organization. At the network level they argue the synapse contributes not only to storage but also to recall, pattern separation, and pattern completion, with plasticity-related structural changes as possible synaptic engrams. Outlook covers mossy-fiber sprouting in epilepsy, 'mossy fiber synaptopathy' in psychiatric models, and early impairment in neurodegenerative disease.
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest the mossy fiber synapse could become the first synapse with a complete account of biophysics, network function, and disease contribution, and a selective therapeutic target; that program is prospective.

summaries.beginner: Deep in the hippocampus, granule cells make unusually large synapses onto CA3 cells. Because those terminals are big enough to record from directly, they have become a test bed for how synapses work and how that shapes memory-related computations.
summaries.intermediate: In Science (2024), Vandael and Jonas review the hippocampal mossy fiber synapse (dentate gyrus granule axons onto CA3 pyramidal dendrites). They synthesize nanoanatomy and nanophysiology—presynaptic and paired patch-clamp, super-resolution light microscopy, freeze-fracture and flash-and-freeze EM—linking facilitation to Ca2+ channel–release-sensor coupling and potentiation to vesicle-pool organization. They argue the synapse contributes to storage, recall, pattern separation, and pattern completion, with structural plasticity as possible synaptic engrams.
summaries.advanced: The on-disk PDF was a mismatch and could not be replaced, so this card follows the catalog abstract. This is a review; biophysical and disease claims summarize the literature rather than a single new experiment. No original sample sizes or effect sizes appear. Therapeutic targeting is prospective.

plain_language_summary: Deep in the hippocampus, granule cells make unusually large synapses onto CA3 cells. Because those terminals are big enough to record from directly, they have become a test bed for how synapses work and how that shapes memory-related computations.

ocar.opportunity: Zooming from synapses (nanometers) through cells (micrometers) to the whole human brain could reveal neuronal connectivity at every scale. Meeting the resulting compute and storage demand may also yield methods useful beyond neuroscience.
ocar.challenge: The adult human brain contains on the order of 86 billion neurons. Linking those spatial scales is most challenging. C. elegans (302 neurons) has a characterized connectome and a proposed structural-functional model; comparable human detail is still a long way off.
ocar.action: Amunts and Lippert write in Science (2021) a perspective on how big data from unraveling human brain structure raise processing demands, tying human connectome decoding to exponentially growing computational and storage technologies.
ocar.resolution: They argue that decoding the human connectome, signal transduction, and relations to brain function is linked to those technology challenges, which in turn may lead to creative solutions beyond neuroscience.
ocar.future_work: The implied program is advancing computational and storage technologies to the scale of human multiscale structural data; specific systems are not named.

summaries.beginner: The human brain has on the order of 86 billion neurons, and linking synapses to the whole organ creates data that strain even supercomputers. This commentary argues that mapping the human connectome will force new computing and storage ideas, which may then help science more broadly.
summaries.intermediate: In Science (2021), Amunts and Lippert discuss how human-brain structural data, spanning synapses (nanometers) through cells (micrometers) to the whole organ, raise processing and storage demands. They contrast the completed C. elegans connectome (302 neurons) and a proposed structural-functional model with the still-distant human case, arguing that decoding the human connectome and linking it to function depends on exponentially growing computational and storage technologies.
